subtopic: REQUEST FOR SECRET SITTING OF THE HOUSE TO CONSIDER RECENT DEVELOPMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in
view of the close proximity of the coast where enemy submarines are now operating, and by reason of particulars I possess and desire to share with the house, but which it would not be wise to disclose publicly, I would ask the government as the representative of the constituency in the vicinity of which these enemy submarine activities are taking place that an immediate secret session of the house be held to consider these most important war developments which are taking place as far as 300 miles within our Atlantic border. These events are of such gravity that it seems to me that the people's representatives should be made aware of all details concerning the attacks and be given an opportunity to take part in deliberations on the means to protect our threatened country.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, with regard to the discussion initiated last evening by the hon. member for Lake Centre as to the director-general of aircraft production, it would appear that the aircraft industry has been in convention in Ottawa yesterday and to-day. and they have sent me a document which I should like to read to the house and place on Hansard. It is dated May 15, 1942, and reads:
Representatives of every phase of the aircraft industry in Canada, assembled in convention at Ottawa, do hereby unanimously resolve that:
1.	They are familiar with the facts connected with the organization of the morale-building campaign, which has resulted in the setting up of a series of advisory committees from coast to coast, consisting of citizens of the highest standing in their communities, and are satisfied that there have been no improper actions taken, and that Mr. E. G. Hirst has received no direct or indirect benefit from his activities in connection with this matter.
2.	They consider this activity to be a well-planned effort to build up and maintain the morale of all workers in the aircraft industry and that its continuance is a vital necessity, in the national interest.
3.	That whereas in the past, this activity has had to be carried on in a somewhat informal manner, funds should be provided to enable it to continue on a formal basis.
4.	They wish to bring to the minister's attention that Ralph P. Bell, as Director-General of Aircraft Production of the Department of

Munitions and Supply, and his organization, have brought the aircraft industry in Canada from a low condition to its present high standard.
5.	That Mr. Bell has given unsparingly of his time and energy to this important phase of the war effort and that he has set a standard of patriotic devotion and duty which is an inspiration to all who have contact with him. Canadian Pratt & Whitney Aircraft Co. Ltd., James Young, President.

This document I think shows definitely that Mr. Bell has been proceeding along the right lines, although his methods in this instance do not commend themselves to myself, or I believe to the house. Apparently there was no doubt that the industry were fully agreed that an officer of the type appointed by Mr. Bell was necessary, and that the organization which is being built up by this officer has been doing most efficient work. You will notice that all firms in the aircraft industry urge that the work be not discontinued, but rather formalized and carried on in an expanded way.
I noticed in reading Hansard that the suggestion was made last evening that Mr. Hirst received a salary from the industry which was charged indirectly to the government.
War Appropriation-Supplies

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No, no; nobody said that.

speechtext:
I think I should make it
clear that he has received only out-of-pocket
expenses.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Nobody said he was receiving a salary. What was said was that he was being reimbursed by business.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: The hon. member for Lake Centre made a remark which led me to believe that that was meant.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Nobody said that.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: In any case I want to make it clear that he received no salary and no indirect pay through advertising.

So far as I am concerned there is no argument about the fine work that is being done and has been done by Mr. Bell. But the minister in bringing this matter up again has not answered the contention which I made last evening that the action taken by the department in this matter was improper. Only a few moments ago I received a telegram which bears out the contention of my leader last evening when he referred to the dangers inherent in this kind of thing. There has been no answer yet to one question which was asked last evening, and to which I think we should have an answer, arising out of that portion of the letter written by the director of aircraft production to the aircraft companies, which reads:
This sum-
That is, the sum advanced by these companies.
-is, by arrangement with treasury, chargeable to overhead in connection with your aircraft contracts.
Before I read the telegram may I ask the minister now when the arrangement with treasury was made, who made it, and generally all the circumstances touching on that arrangement.
My criticism last night was twofold: first, why conceal this item; second, why not have revealed the circumstances to parliament when the question with regard thereto was first asked? Last night my leader pointed out the dangers inherent in this thing, and he asked the minister specifically whether this was the only case of its kind; are there others? As yet there is no answer to that.
The telegram which I received to-day is dated May 15 and is from Toronto. It reads as follows:
A letter signed "Bell" of Department Munitions and Supply soliciting business for E. G. Hirst was sent not only to aircraft factories but to commercial firms including a
War Appropriation-Supplies

number of our customers. We have reason to believe we lost at least one substantial contract from an organization which needs government good will because of this letter.
Millways, Toronto.
First, why the concealment; why was not this man shown on the records as receiving a total amount of $9,000 in expenses? It was being paid by the government of Canada. Second, are there others in the same position as Mr. Hirst? Third, why was this course adopted instead of revealing the matter either by showing his name as an employee or showing that his expenses were chargeable to the people of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I think it has been made perfectly clear that I did not know of the transaction. As a matter of fact I knew of it about a week after the leader of the opposition knew about it. An employee leaving the company sent a letter to the leader of the opposition, and the new incumbent sent it to me because it had been sent to the leader of the opposition. That is the first I knew of it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I shall have to correct that. Nobody sent me the letter. It was sent to a colleague of mine who brought it to me.
If the minister will allow me-I have to go in a minute-I should like to say that nobody at any time has attempted to disparage Mr. Bell's activity as aircraft director. I want to make that perfectly clear. I agree entirely with the minister that the method he adopted was reprehensible and that the practice should be stopped, and stopped at once, and the money returned to everybody who contributed. If they want to build up a morale campaign let them go about it in the right way and do it in the right way, but do not let the cost of it be smuggled into the expenditures of the taxpayers of Canada under the guise of an addition to overhead. If it is a necessary expenditure, by all means let us make it.
How many other schemes of this kind are being financed indirectly, secretly, by the treasury' of Canada, the taxpayers not knowing the slightest thing about it? If there are any, let us have the names at once; if there are none, then let us know.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I know of no others. I did not know of this one until it turned up by accident, but I do not think that after the impropriety was called to Mr. Bell's attention there will be the slightest possibility that it will be repeated. As I said last night, it was not a matter of charging expenditures to overhead. Instructions had gone out that that should not be done and it has not been done. I think this matter
should be dropped. The only purpose would be further to smear his name across the headlines of the country. It has gone from coast to coast, and I doubt if it adds to the war effort. However, it was done. I made it clear that what was done was done with the acquiescence of the trade, and the results won the endorsement of the trade as indicated by the statement I have put on Hansard.

During the time the Department of Munitions and Supply will be before the committee I am going to try to find out if it is possible, first, to increase aircraft production; second, what the situation is with regard to the production of synthetic rubber; third, what the situation re magnesium metal is; fourth, whether by some means Canada can bring about the production of oil in a big way.
I had intended commencing with No. 1, aircraft production, but in view of what took place yesterday and again to-day I will delay my remarks on that subject and begin by discussing the possibility of producing oil on a large scale in the dominion. I believe that either the branch of the oil controller published a number of advertisements on December 2, or that such advertisements were published on their behalf. I have one here which reads:
The empire's mechanized forces rolling on to victory need oil, war's greatest weapon.
The advertisement illustrates a couple of tanks and is well adapted for attracting the attention of people to the necessity of conserving oil. On September 25, 1941, the director of public information issued a bulletin in which these words appear:
Oil and the war.
"The Battle for Oil" is the title of the latest film release of the national film board. One of the "Canada Carries On" series, it shows the vital part played by gasoline and oil in modern war.
Then the minister's own department on the 12th instant issued a bulletin in which I find these words:
Canada's gasoline inventory is steadily becoming worse.
On March 24, the minister himself made a speech which was reported in the Globe and Mail. I do not know the name of the club or the body whom he addressed, but his speech was reported in the Globe and Mail and he made a frank statement on the subject. He said:
If I tell you frankly that we are likely to lose the war unless we can get enough oil and enough rubber you will understand how very serious our position is.

War Appropriation-Supplies
That was a frank statement which should command the attention not only of the people of Canada but of all those who are interested in the production of oil, which, as I read a moment ago, is the war's greatest weapon. Then in Hansard of November 20, 1940, the minister made a statement which indicated that at that time he had in mind the production of oil in Canada. As reported at page 268 of Hansard of November 20, 1940, he said:
The oil controller first of all addressed himself to the problem of ascertaining the exact position of the petroleum industry in Canada, with a view to assuring an adequate supply of petroleum products for military purposes, and also to determine the production capacity of Canadian sources of supply, which are largely confined to the province of Alberta.
From that it is clearly evident that the subject of oil production has been under the consideration of the minister and his department almost from the beginning. What has been done since that statement was made in 1940 or since the war broke out to bring about the production of oil in Canada on a large scale?
I believe that some time around 1914 oil was discovered in Turner valley. Perhaps it was earlier than that, but that was about the time the first well was tapped. A fine job is being done there. Relatively speaking, it is a small field, comprising about 10,000 acres with a capacity, I am told, of approximately
10,000	barrels an acre or a total capacity of 100,000,000 barrels. Comparatively
100,000,000 barrels would be considered a small oil field, as I say, they are doing a fine job and their oil is good. Their products are good. I have been over the plant, and I think they are producing about 26,000 barrels a day. Naturally, owing to the size of the field, I believe they are proceeding in the right direction in not trying to develop all their oil at once. I believe that during the last few years various oil companies have been drilling in different areas of Saskatchewan, and others in Alberta. Some oil is being developed near the Alberta-Saskatchewan boundary at a place called Vermilion. The quantity produced is not large but it is developing. In Ontario, oil was first sought for in 1859 near Collingwood, but nothing has ever come of it. I am told, however, that recently oil geologists have been in the area again trying to ascertain if there is any source of oil there worth tapping. The counties of Lambton and Kent in the early sixties did produce quite a quantity of oil for those days. I believe it was about 1861 that they commenced producing oil in the county of
Lambton; it spread into the county of Kent, and for three years they produced a total of approximately 3,000,000 barrels of oil. Many lion, members have been through that area and have seen oil-well derricks still standing. They have been standing there for many years. Lately, attempts have been made to tap a few more wells there, and I believe they are producing oil, but not very much.
I am told that at present oil geologists are in New Brunswick, as were oil geologists in 1858 and thereabouts. At that time the place was called Baltimore. I am not just sure of the location. I talked to one engineer who was familiar with the oil shales of New Brunswick, and he said he thought something might come out of investigations there.
Last summer I made a trip to the Peace River area and learned that some years ago, about 1921, oil wells were discovered not very far from the town of Peace River, but not much came of that. I have read the reasons but will not take time to relate them now. From what I read in a letter from Mr. H. A. George of Peace River I would say there is a fair amount of oil in that neighbourhood.
During the last few years oil has been found at Fort Norman on the Mackenzie river and is being produced, although not in a large way. I tried to go to Fort Norman last summer but did not. I expect to go this summer if the house rises in time for me to obtain transportation down the Mackenzie river. The oil wells there produce first-class oil. There is a small refinery there. I believe the product is largely consumed by the mines roundabout. Geologists tell me a large amount of oil is obtainable there.
This brings me to the area about which I desire to speak at some length, the oil sand area at present being developed on the Horse river about a mile and a half from Fort McMurray and extending down the Athabasca river for some sixty miles and on the Clearwater river and the Christine river, but the focal point, as far as I can see from investigations covering some days up and down these rivers, is near Fort McMurray. Later I am going to ask the minister-I will ask it now to give it more emphasis-to request the appointment of a board of engineers from government departments to investigate thoroughly all data pertaining to the oil possibilities of the Athabasca river area, and if they are found to be, as so many say they are, of tremendous importance, that the government take steps to bring about production of oil in that area in a large way. I intend to say more on that later. I know some of the departments, particularly the Department

War Appropriation-Supplies

of Mines and Resources, have as capable oil geologists as there are anywhere in America. I have had many conversations with Doctor
S.	C. Ells, and in my opinion there is not a better oil geologist anywhere or one who has made more extensive surveys and studied the subject of production of oil more than Doctor Ells. There are other men maybe as good, but I am better acquainted with Doctor Ells. What I suggest at present is that these men in the government service, who must know whether there is oil in a big way at or along the Athabasca river and how those oil resources can be developed, be asked to promote that development as a board or committee or however the minister decides.
It is no wonder that the oil controller's branch, or whoever publishes the advertisements under that branch, said that oil is war's greatest munition. It is because of that fact and because their oil requirements are so tremendous that the Germans are to-day sending their legions through the Kerch peninsula on their way to the Caucasus. Prior to the war the German requirements were about seventy million barrels a year; to-day they exceed two hundred million barrels, and unless the Germans have a tremendous reserve beyond all conception they must be nearly out of oil. I hope they are. But if they are getting nearly out, that of course would be their incentive in driving toward the Caucasus mountains.
What are our own requirements. The Canadian army is not of very great size yet. It will be larger. But the "Imperial Oil Review" of recent date states that we have 23,500 military vehicles burning gasoline, and they estimate the requirements of Canada's 23,500 vehicles at 100,000 gallons a day, whether they are operating or not. I presume they mean that when those vehicles are operating it will take a great deal more than that, but to lay up reserves they estimate 100.000 gallons a day.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: That is the army in Canada alone, I take it.
I am saying what the "Imperial Oil Review" states, that Canada's army is rolling along on 23,500 vehicles.
In Canada or out?
I do not know. They are not rolling much outside yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: We have a far larger number of vehicles overseas with our army.

I am glad to hear that.
That makes the demands on Canada's oil production evidently greater than 100,000 gallons a day. fMr. MacNicol.]

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Yes. I want to make it clear that that refers to the figure for Canada.

That means all the more necessity for Canada to obtain oil of its own if it can. The same article states that an infantry division to-day requires 249,000 horsepower, which is twice the horse-power used in the industries of the city of Hamilton, and that an armoured division requires 387,000 horse-power, about the equivalent of that used in Toronto for peak-load light and power. This goes to show that the demand is tremendous and is bound to increase, because we as a country have not yet done anything as far as equipment being in active combat is concerned. When it does get into active combat it will render as good an account of itself as any.
Some days ago I read a statement that the average battleship, 35,000 to 45,000 tons, would require at one refuelling from 750,000 to
1,000,000 gallons of oil. Therefore ships on the water are going to require a tremendous amount of oil.
The other night the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power), whom I always like to see in his seat and to hear when he is piloting his estimates through the house, because he is always so courteous and so willing to answer questions, said that the present air demands for gasoline have increased from $9,000,000 last year-in Canada I presume?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: In Canada.

-to $20,000,000 this year. If we now require $20,000,000 worth a year in Canada, turned into barrels that is quite an item.
In Regina there is a very capable engineer, Mr. C. Gower of Regina, with whom I had the pleasure of being last summer in the Athabasca oil area vicinity, who estimates that the amount of gasoline that will come from 600 barrels of raw oil is 270 barrels. Using that as a basis, it means that $20,000,000 worth of gasoline would be the equivalent of approximately 4,444,444 barrels of oil. That is more than one-half of Canada's production to-day. In other words, approximately one-half of the oil produced in Canada to-day would be required to operate the aeroplanes the minister was speaking about. If he did not include the aeroplanes that are in Europe, then it would be much more. There is a tremendous necessity to use our resources to the utmost.
I referred a moment ago to what the Germans required, 200,000,000 barrels a year.
I have no doubt that Great Britain requires

War Appropriation-Supplies
approximately the same amount. Great Britain has been getting her oil from several sources, the Dutch East Indies, her own supplies in Sarawak, from Burma, Borneo, from Bahrein island, from Iran and Iraq and some from Egypt. What is the position of the oil supplies from these fields to-day? Apart from prosecuting the war, the main reason the Japs went south was the need for oil. Japan produces only about 2,500,000 barrels of oil a year, but it is quite likely that her war machine requires half as much as the German war machine. An additional supply of 75,000,000 to 100,000,000 barrels would be worth while to Japan. What did Japan gain by taking Java, Borneo, Sarawak and Burma? She gained all that production, and if she gets into India she will get a little more. All those supplies are now lost to the allies.
I hope the Germans will not win in their mad race toward the Caucasus but perhaps it would be worth while to conjecture what would happen if they get through. In the Caucasus they would be able to get 225,000,000 barrels a year. If they got that far, it is quite possible they might get into Iran and Iraq, where another 105,000,000 barrels a year would be available. If they got into Iraq, they would probably get Bahrein island, which produces about 7,000,000 barrels a year. Then they might even get into Egypt, where another 6,000,000 barrels a year is produced.
I like to look the situation in the face. If the Germans get all these countries I have just mentioned they will have available 343,000,000 barrels a year which is now available to the allies. The only supplies left to the allies then would be north and south America. On these continents the British have only Trinidad and the Canadian production. The Canadian production now is about 9,000,000 barrels a year, while the Trinidad production is approximately 20,000,000 barrels a year. Outside of that combined production of 29,000,000 barrels a year they would have to go to Venezuela, Peru and the United States. Happily the United States produces more oil than all the rest of the world, her production being something like 1,350,000,000 barrels a year. If Great Britain must rely on the production in Canada and Trinidad, which is only 29,000,000 barrels a year, it is all the more imperative that Canada should produce all the oil possible.
In the early days of the last century and up to now oil came from wells. I remember not so many years ago that gold was taken only from the mouths of rivers, from the sands. Then someone discovered the cyanide
44561-157}
process which permitted gold to be taken out of the rock, and since that time more gold has been produced than in all the world's history. We have some very bright engineers in our departments; some of them may discover a method of extracting oil from sand faster than at present, and this process may have the same effect upon the production of oil from the oil sands as the cyanide process had upon the production of gold from quartz.
During the last two or three years I have read everything I could find about the production of oil from sand, and I consulted with as many engineers as I could come in contact with. Last summer I went to see these oil-sand areas. I like to see things for myself; I never can get very enthusiastic about anything unless I can see it. What did I find? I found a small plant on the Horse river near Fort McMurray. This plant has since burned down, but I believe it has been erected again and is now in operation or will be shortly. Last summer it was producing about 250 barrels a day. These oil-sands are quite black, as hon. members can see from the piece I have in my hand. I was present when this particular piece was blasted. If one holds a piece in his fingers for a moment they become covered with oil. It is made up of millions of minute pieces of sand, with a small film of oil around each piece.
At Fort McMurray the sands are about forty feet thick. The engineers told me, and this has been confirmed by the departmental engineers, that in the immediate vicinity of the plant there are several million barrels of oil that can be taken out by the open cut method. The top soil, which is ordinary dirt, is removed with a steam shovel, and you come at once in contact with a depth of forty feet of solid black oil-sands, every cubic yard of which contains approximately one barrel of prime crude oil.
In order to make sure that it produced prime diesel oil I went down to Great Slave lake and lake Athabasca where they told me that the oil is being used in their diesel engines. The engineers at the mines on Great Slave lake, in the vicinity of Yellowknife, and the engineers in the mines at Goldfields on lake Athabasca, told me that there was no better oil anywhere, and that they had given orders to the producing company to ship them every barrel of oil they could. That convinced me that it was good oil. If it were not, these engineers would not have asked for it. If there were anything wrong with the oil it would ruin the engines. I brought down a small bottle of the diesel oil. You see it is black, but it is mighty good stuff. I also brought down a small bottle of the gasoline. It is amazing, when we realize that gasoline
War Appropriation-Supplies

comes out of a solid black sand like that. This is 70 octane. They can raise it a good deal higher, as other companies do; but they tell me it comes through at about 70. Whether that is so or not, I cannot say; I am just taking their word for it.
This shows, however, that the material is in those sands. The question is as to the quantity and whether it would be worth while for the government to assist somebody in producing oil there in a big way. In reply to a question, I heard the minister say on February 18:
I have a very exhaustive report on the subject of tar sands, and I should be very glad to let my hon. friend have a copy of it. It indicates, however, that the location of the sands and the possibility of development is too remote to be of any great use in this war.

Can they produce high-testing
gasoline?

Yes. What I have read is the minister's opinion, and I find no fault with it; it is not mine. Fort McMurray is 305 miles from Edmonton. By direct pipeline I suppose it is not more than 250 miles. At sixty miles down the river it would be only about 300 miles from Edmonton, and that is not far for a pipeline. It is, in fact, a short pipeline. We are bringing oil now from Oklahoma to Sarnia, a distance of not much less than a thousand miles. The British pipeline from Iran and Iraq to Beirut is not, I should think, any less than a thousand miles.
If we have the heart to produce oil in Canada, and if it is there-and our engineers say it is-then we should be producing it. We are now producing only about 9,000,000 barrels or less a year from all our fields, and I believe we have over 10,000 wells in Canada-or, I should say, we have had that many. I believe there are not as many now, but the fact is that from all our wells in Canada we are now producing about 9,000,000 barrels a year. However, we are buying not less than 50,000,000 barrels a year. A little later on I shall quote a great engineer's statement to the effect that the time may come when the oil wells will stop flowing. Let us remember in that connection that the oil sands would not stop producing their oil. According to our own engineers, their supply is inexhaustible.
What does our own expert, Doctor S. C. Ells, have to say on the subject? May I say in passing that he is one of the best officials with which any government has ever been blessed. I could enlarge upon that statement by saying that the more I meet our permanent civil servants, the more I am convinced that Canada has in her civil service very fine men
fMr. MacNicol.]
and women. They are as good as the best, and thoroughly seized with the desire to serve
Canada.
Doctor Ells says this:
Commencing in 1913-
I believe that is when the doctor commenced to make the investigation.
-the writer undertook an investigation of the bituminous sands of northern Alberta. The results of this work, subsequently extending over a period of some fifteen years, have appeared in numerous publications issued from time to time by the mines branch. The work undertaken and the results obtained, supplemented by laboratory studies by officers of the fuel testing division, may be briefly summarized as follows:
(a)	The general character of the bituminous sand over a large area has been studied and many samples taken. These samples have been analysed and the physical and chemical characteristics of the sand and of the associated bitumen determined.
(b)	Detailed topographical surveys of areas aggregating 1,260 square miles adjacent to Athabasca river and its tributaries have been completed.
That is a fairly extensive investigation. I believe that since that time some 10,000 to
15,000	square miles have been covered. I do not mean that the whole 10,000 or 15,000 square miles are rich in oil, like the sands at Fort McMurray. They are not, in fact; but there is a lot of oil in them. Whereas at Fort McMurray some of the sand fields are only forty feet deep, in other areas they extend to depths of 100, 150 or 200 feet. This goes to show that it is by far the most stupendous oil field in the world.
To quote further from Doctor Ells:
Upwards of 5,000 tons of bituminous sand has been excavated by the mines branch in connection with experimental work, affording information as to the methods best adapted for the mining of this class of material.
That was fairly good ground with which to experiment. At the present time the oil-sand in the area at Fort McMurray, on the Horse river, is being blasted. The engineer in charge while I was there, a man named John Byrum, for whom I developed a warm regard, seemed to be thoroughly posted. He told me that only a period of two minutes elapsed between the time I saw the sand in the pit until I saw the oil being taken off Then, in about twenty minutes the oil is poured back to the refineries, and within seventy minutes it is refined. This goes to show that it is a very rapid process, almost as fast as pumping oil out of a well. I do not want anyone to think I am not proud of our oil wells in Canada, because I am. I would not want anyone to think I am opposed to taking oil from wells, because I am not.

War Appropriation-Supplies
If we have oil in sands, and can produce it, then I maintain we should produce it.
Doctor Ells goes on to say:
A study has been made of a number of processes designed for the recovery of the hydrocarbons from bituminous sand and results indicate that recovery can be readily effected by the use of heated water.
That is the way it is done. It is, in fact, a very simple process. The sand goes into a large revolving tank containing hot water at about ISO degrees. The tank revolves, and the hot water has a disintegrating effect on the oil sand. The product then goes into settling basins where it is again agitated, and in due course the oil comes through. Doctor Ells continues:
In the light of information now available it is clear that bituminous sand should be seriously regarded as an important potential source of solid and liquid hydrocarbons-
And of a long list of chemicals which follows in its wake. One of these chemicals is the ingredient required in connection with the production of synthetic rubber, which I shall discuss at a later stage.
He continues:
Actually it is as yet impossible to estimate accurately the potential production of petroleum
Firoduets that may ultimately become available rom Alberta bituminous sands. It is however known that that area underlaid by bituminous sand is not less than 1,500 square miles and the total area extent of the deposit is probably much greater.
And then the following:
Meanwhile results of field investigations by the mines branch indicate that at least
750,000,000 tons of bituminous sand can be mined by open-cut methods.
All these reports must be available to the minister. Perhaps these are the ones to which he referred the other day. Doctor Ells continues:
On a basis of 12 per cent bitumen content this is equivalent to 90,000,000 tons of bitumen or 500,000,000 barrels.
That has been enlarged to a billion barrels of oil.
Then, Mr. Max Ball, president of Abasand oil company, makes the statement in quoting Doctor Ells that the area contains a hundred billion barrels of oil. He is referring not to the Fort McMurray area, but to the whole area as far as the Peace river. He goes on to quote the United States bureau of mines, which places the figure at 250,000,000,000 barrels of oil. I think I have quoted enough to justify the statement that there is an enormous quantity of oil there, constituting a most valuable resource if a 100 per cent economical method is found to get it out. I make no comment on that, but they say
that they can produce refined oil at $1.36 a barrel at the mines. Then taken out to Edmonton, it might reach a couple of dollars. Perhaps I should not quote these figures because I am not certain of them. Several other authorities have visited the area, including Doctor T. O. Bosworth, who was chief geologist of Imperial Oil, Limited, and he made the following statement:
In the district of McMurray on the Athabasca river, we have the largest natural exposure of oil in the world.^ It is interesting to consider the amount of oil in this territory. For this purpose we will suppose the area to be 15,000 square miles-
That is higher than Doctor Ells' estimate. -and the average thickness fifty feet.
That is a lot of oil. The Alberta government estimates the bituminous sands of northern Alberta to contain 100,000,000,000 barrels of oil, while the United States bureau of mines places the figure at 250,000,000,000 barrels. An engineer named Gustav Egloff, of the Universal Oil Products company, in a speech delivered to the American Institute of Chemical Engineers at Birmingham, Alabama, had this to say:
One of the greatest known hydrocarbon deposits in the world to-day is that of the Canadian Alberta bituminous sands. The known bituminous sand deposits are estimated to contain over 100,000,000,000 barrels of bitumen.
I think I have quoted sufficient to indicate that men who should be competent to judge, including our own engineers, are convinced that there is a very large deposit of oil there. I see my time is about up, and I shall conclude with just one more quotation. Referring to drilling for oil wells, the chief geologist for the Anglo-Iranian Oil company is quoted as saying in January, 1940:
Using all geological and geophysical assistance, the average chance of success cannot be rated on a basis of experience, as better than one in ten. The new interest now being taken by American companies is based on the belief that American oil resources will not stand the present rate of production for many years.
Nobody can tell how long because oil wells give out. Again I would urge the minister to have the best engineers in the government service get together to make a survey and study the possibilities of developing oil in immense quantities from the sands of Alberta. I have talked with a number of them and I know they would be glad to do it. It is, of course, immaterial to me personally who develops these resources. I believe the government engineers should cooperate with the oil producers and say to them: "Here, gentlemen, are our reports." The government should then say to these producers: "We will give you so many square miles of these oil
247S
War Appropriation-Supplies

resources, and you can go to it and produce the oil."
With regard to getting the oil out, it is not far, only 305 miles, to Edmonton. A pipeline of 250 miles in length would cost about $2,500,000. Again, it is only 800 miles to Prince Rupert. Calgary is only 450 miles away. The oil could be piped to Calgary, it could be pumped to Winnipeg, 700 miles away, and refined there too. The oil could also be taken to Churchill by pipeline; then taken by tankers to Moosonee, at the south end of James bay, and from there it could be brought by pipeline to Toronto, 900 miles away. We have in these oil deposits hundreds of billions of barrels of oil, but even if it were only hundreds of millions it would pay this country to develop these resources and become an exporter instead of an- importer of oil.
One last word, Mr. Chairman, and I thank you for your courtesy. Before this war broke out there was an article in the press which stated that the German government or somebody representing the German government desired to run a pipeline from the oil fields of western Canada to the Pacific coast. Manifestly they had no intention of running a pipeline from Turner valley because no one would put in a pipeline of that length to transport
100,000,000 barrels of oil. I had the good fortune to meet a Mr. Goffatt who told me he had met the German oil geologist who investigated here in Canada after the geologist had just returned from the Athabasca area. They met on the train from Edmonton. During the course of their conversation the German geologist became tremendously excited over the immense possibilities that he saw in that region. That was in 1911 or 1912. The German geologist went back to Germany and came out again to this country in 1914; he was about to plan oil production when the war broke out, and that put an end to the matter as far as the German geologist was concerned. But the point I make is that the German geologist had been searching for oil all over the world and had arrived at the conclusion that this was the greatest deposit of oil anywhere in the world. I am not an oil engineer or an oil geologist, but I am interested in investigating and I do not mind what it costs me to travel in the course of an investigation. The only reason why I am here at all is to try to serve my native land. There is nothing in this personally for me. If I cannot do something for Canada when I am here, I am going to quit this house. I have no interest only to serve the country itself in which I was born.

I do not ask the minister for an answer now, but I do ask him to think over what I have said and look over the reports he has, and then to appoint a board of our own engineers to investigate these resources. If the deposits are there in such immense amounts as we are informed they are, let us take any legitimate means under the sun that are required to bring about the production of oil in Canada so that we may become an exporter instead of an importer of oil, and further, in order that we may be of vital help to the empire in the event of all other sources of oil being cut off except those within the empire itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I wish to thank the hon. member for Davenport for the constructive contribution he has made to the debate and for the valuable information he has put on Hansard. The position of oil development within Canada has, of course, been changed considerably by the events of recent months. I think most people had looked upon the tar sands of Alberta as a great reserve of oil for some future period when the more easily accessible oil resources would have been exhausted. But to-day we think of that same area as a source of immediate oil production, provided the problems connected with its development can be solved rapidly and with some degree of certainty.
An intensive study of the tar sands is under way at the present time. That study was organized by my department, and we have interested in it the leading oil engineers of this country, not only men in the public service and on the staff of the national research council, but also oil engineers from industry. We have interested Consolidated Mining and Smelting, who have had a good deal of experience in meeting mining problems in that area.
I may say that the mining of the sand itself is one of the major problems that has not yet been fully worked out. We have asked all these interests to prepare a report for the government and advise whether a development should be undertaken at this time and the extent of development which the conditions would warrant, whether we should proceed with a pilot plant or whether the situation is such that we can immediately develop on a considerable scale. I am expecting the report shortly, and appropriate action will be taken.
The government is also exploring the New Brunswick shale deposits to which reference has been made. The difficulty with this deposit was that until recently it was under the control of private interests. However, the

War Appropriation-Supplies
New Brunswick government have now secured the title, and the federal government is in partnership with the provincial government in making a thorough exploration of these shales to determine the probable quantity of oil available and the pertinent facts in relation to its development.
Arrangements have been made to develop further the wells on the lower Mackenzie at Fort Norman. Additional wells are being drilled, the refinery capacity is being increased, and a short pipeline is being installed to bring the oil across to the location of the Alaska highway.
There are proceeding with the government of British Columbia conversations which, we hope, will lead to an immediate and thorough exploration of the Peace River block of British Columbia, which is regarded as a very probable source of oil, and which is conveniently located to the railway for use on the Pacific coast.
I mention this to indicate that I share my hon. friend's interest in finding oil within Canada, and we hope that some constructive progress can be made before I report to parliament again.

Mr. Chairman, may I first congratulate you upon your gracious act yesterday in giving place to one of the fair ladies of this house? We in this corner say, "Do it again".
Before I came to this house I thought a good deal and said much about public ownership and who should share the profits. I knew then, as I know now, that any enterprise must have four parts: there must be the money or the capital to put into the enterprise; there must be the brains or the management to run it; there must be the men who will do the work, and there must be the consumer. I still believe that the man who toils should have his share of the profit; and my first observation with regard to the Department of Munitions and Supply is that I appreciate very much the way in which they have branched out into public ownership. There was nothing like it before in Canada: we now have full-fledged government owned companies manufacturing munitions, chemicals, aircraft equipment, and building ships. These are known as:
1.	Allied War Supplies Corporation.
2.	Fairmont Company Limited.
3.	Plateau Company.
4.	Small Arms Limited.
5.	Federal Aircraft Limited.
6.	Toronto Shipbuilding Company.
7.	Wartime Merchant Shipping Limited.
8.	Atlas Plant Extension Limited.
9.	Wartime Housing Limited.
10.	Research Enterprises Limited.
11.	Melbourne Merchandising Limited.
12.	Citadel Merchandising Company Limited.
I would say that these are the twelve apostles in pioneering along this line, in doing a job and filling a gap which could not have been filled by private enterprise, and I understand that there is more to follow.
Another thing I like about this department has to do with the announcement which was made the other day when the committee on war expenditures was being set up. The note was sounded, and very clearly, by two ministers, the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson), that "we have nothing to hide." I am sure the people of Canada welcome that statement.
I wish to make a suggestion which touches a tender spot. Somebody else has thought along the same lines, but perhaps it has not been put forward in the right way; perhaps, too, I may not do so. Near our aeroplane manufacturing plant at Fort William we have across the road a military training centre where there are about 300 men. There are two chaplains, one Protestant and one Roman Catholic, to look after these men. Just across the street is this plant, with about 5,000 men and women. I know that they have in this plant a splendid staff of matrons, good and efficient women. But I do believe that since these men. because of their work, which is done on Sundays as well as week days, are unable to get the benefits which are available to the ordinary citizen, there might be men appointed-call them chaplains if you will- by the Department of National Defence or the government of Canada who would meet these men at the noon hour and talk good Christian democratic common sense to them and give them something to think about which will encourage them to sweat up to their jobs and do the work the minister expects them to do.
Another thing I should like to speak about is the way in which these plants are looked after from headquarters. First, I would mention a small shell factory, the only one which was opened up locally since the war started. It has a contract to turn out 1,000 shells of about fiftyjiounds each a day; it has been turning out l,o00 a day, and those in charge are anxious to extend the plant. Why are they capable of this production? It is because the workers have the will to work and the management have the heart to back up the men in their work. There is thorough cooperation. The only difficulty I ever noticed was when two young ladies of the inspection staff said that they thought they should be paid more money-and I agreed with them. They were getting 33 to 35 cents an hour while other girls were getting 45 cents up,
War Appropriation-Supplies

and money paid by the government does not go any further than money earned in any other way. However, thanks to the action of the Minister of Labour, as soon as a girl is competent to earn, she will be paid according to her efficiency.
I know something about the car works. I practically grew up with its development. I believe it was in November, 1935, that I received an announcement from the late president that the plant would be opening. Of course I was anxious that it should be opened, because in 1935 we had many idle men; I did everything possible, and I bothered the Minister of Munitions and Supply a good deal. He was always courteous, and just as anxious as I was to have the car works opened. A year later, I believe early in 1937, the plant was being prepared for the building of aeroplanes. There were great difficulties to be overcome. They had great difficulties in the first year or two. It was not much better than a big school training young fellows from Fort William, Port Arthur and the surrounding districts, and they did it well. They wanted to make planes for Trans-Canada Air Lines, and I shall not forget the remarks of the minister when the executive in room 16 met him. He said, "If you can get the right to make a plane that has been tested and tried you will get an order; we are not out to take any risks with Trans-Canada Air Lines." He was wise.
I have found the management of Canada Car most courteous, kind and trustful toward me. In fact, they will allow me to visit that plant any day I have time and they will not send a guard to see that I conduct myself properly. I have seen a big corner at one time where young people were taken in and trained and paid 25 cents an hour, and when they were fit to do filing metal parts properly they were taken into the plant and their wages were increased. They cooperated thoroughly with the vocational school, and lent them equipment, and at one time the vocational school contracted to give them 1,500 partly trained young people by the first of June, 1941. The vocational school measured up splendidly and has been doing that ever since.
There is a union in that plant which has been doing things I never knew a trades union to do before. When anyone is ill and needs to go away they take charge, if necessary, and pay all his expenses. I have known them to pay sickness and funeral expenses in several instances. That shows that union 719 has a heart. It is also progressive. They produce a paper called The Effort, and one

of the fine literary contributors has been, or at any rate will be, the present Minister of Munitions and Supply.
The first Hurricane that was made in Canada was made in Fort William, and it compared favourably with any made in England. I was proud to be at the testing of that plane, because it was a thrilling moment.
Certain things have been said about Canada Car which bother me a little and I am not satisfied until I see my way through anything. I have great respect for the member for Davenport (Mr. MacNieol). I think he has fine judgment and he has made many worthy contributions to this house. I hope he will be long spared to do the same. But I should like to quote what the hon. member said as reported at page 2352 of Hansard:
That factory was building Hurricane bombers. I believe they were turning out about a hundred a month. They may have been turning those planes out for an English order; I do not know. However, for lack of orders they shut down on bombers, and remained shut down for six or seven months. This means that aeroplane facilities, for both defence and attack, for Great Britain and her allies, are short by six or seven hundred bombers they should have had-and could have had. Those bombers could have been made in Fort William. The plant has now started again producing.
I think I know the car works in Fort William, and if they stopped making bombers I am sure I would know about it. I do not think they have ever done so, but I am ready to stand corrected. I received a letter from the highest authority along this line after the announcement of the new order that came to Canada Car for 1,000 Curtis navy dive bombers. He writes:
The production of new aeroplanes will require extensive tooling which will be placed in hand immediately.
That was January 24.
Pending bringing the new planes into production. the Fort William plant will continue to produce the maximum number of Hurricane aircraft.
That means that they have not stopped. I have no doubt, however, that the minister can answer this much better than I can. I have heard members say in this house that there were idle workers. I know there are men in the Canada Car who must be idle, because you cannot keep them busy all the time. Take young fellows who run from one part of the plant to another carrying materials; you cannot keep them always busy but they must be there to carry on. They have to obey their orders promptly when issued. I have stood in an elevated position and looked down on those massive works, and I am sure that if anyone could

War Appropriation-Supplies
see much idleness there I would have seen it.
I congratulate the management of that plant upon the splendid work they have done and the harmony that prevails in the plant at the present time.
The minister took time off to meet the executive of union 719. They had some difficulties because they had heeded certain rumors, but they showed wisdom in going to the minister, and he had no trouble in dispelling the rumors. The result was that they went away satisfied and said, "We have a great Minister of Munitions and Supply".
The other day I listened to the member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) as he said something about a submarine in the St. Lawrence. I am surprised at him when I think how the Department of Munitions and Supply is furnishing materials for every part of the world that is engaged with us in the war. If the hon. member for Temiscouata knows the manly art as I know it, he must know that when a man squares up to you, you will not let him get near enough to trip you up but will hit him before he gets close. That is what we ought to do, and the hon. member for Temiscouata and the group associated with him should change their minds and attack the enemy before he gets into the St. Lawrence. He should be stopped before he gets there. I suppose that if a submarine came up the Rideau canal his attitude would be different.
We must cooperate with the Department of Munitions and Supply with a view to keeping the enemy at a distance. I congratulate the minister upon the work he has done, and I hope he will take as coolly as possible any criticism which I may offer.

I am not going to follow the hon. member who has just spoken except to say that the more aeroplanes we can turn out at this particular time, the better it will be for our war effort. I was disturbed some time ago by stories I had heard of the export of planes from Canada to countries that are neutral now but that may not be friendly neutral, or even neutral, if Hitler should march toward them. In order to clear up these rumours I asked some questions which were answered recently. The questions were:
1.	Have any planes, particularly Fleets 16, been supplied since June 1, 1941, to countries which were, or are, neutral?
2.	If so, to what countries and in what numbers ?
I was surprised at the answers that were given because I was inclined to believe that the stories I had heard were merely rumours. They questions were answered thus:
1. Since June 1, 1941, one export permit has been granted for the export of aircraft from Canada to countries other than the British empire and the United States. The permit in question was granted on August 23, 1941, and covered 18 Douglas bombers owned by the Roval Norwegian Air Force and sold by them to the government of Peru. The planes were at no time the property of the government of Canada, and were only exported after being found unsuitable for the purposes of the RC.A.F. and R.A.F., to whom they were first offered when the Royal Norwegian Air Force found them not suited to their requirements.
It strikes me as strange that Douglas bombers of any type could not have been used somewhere in connection with our own war effort. Having regard to the stories of the fighting at Singapore, Rangoon and elsewhere in the far east-we were told that on one occasion shortly before the fall of Singapore a fighter pilot went into the air in a machine described as an old crate and endeavoured to fight up-to-date Japanese machines-I felt that if we had in Canada planes of any type we should surely have used them in our own war effort rather than allow them to be sent to some other country.	_
Secondly I was told that immediately prior to June, 1941, a permit was granted for the export of ten model 16 Fleet trainers to Portugal for the use of the Portuguese navy. This export took place following consultation with the government of the United Kingdom, in view of the friendly relations existing with Portugal.
The question arises whether the policy followed in this matter by our government over a considerable period was a proper one. For years we were exporting raw material to countries with which we are now at war. Only recently we were permitting large quantities of copper, scrap iron and nickel to go to Japan. Now, of course, having sown the wind we are reaping the whirlwind. In my opinion, until the needs of the united nations are completely met, we have an excellent reason for refusing to supply neutral countries with war equipment that we may need ourselves. A few minutes ago the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) referred to the complaint of the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) the other day that we had not been able to sight and stop the submarine in the St. Lawrence river. Perhaps such criticism is not fully justified; there is something in it. Surely planes of the kind to which I have referred, or at least the engines of those planes, could be utilized for patrol work along our own coasts, even if they were
War Appropriation-Supplies

not suitable for use in battle across the seas. I urge upon the government that they put a stop to this policy of exporting to neutral countries equipment and supplies which we ourselves may need.
We are not permitted to be given the figures as to exports of vital materials. We have been disturbed, for example, about shipments of antimony to neutral powers which at some time in the not far distant future might embarrass us because of their attitude in this war. We have no guarantee that some of these raw materials are not being transhipped from neutral countries or are not replacing similar material that is being shipped to nations with which we are at war. As one who was in Portugal for a few days last November I could not help observing that in the city of Lisbon there was a large number of Germans, with whom from time to time we rubbed shoulders, and that propaganda theatres were operating, open only to neutrals or nationals not unfriendly to the Germans. The hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman) and I one Saturday afternoon tried to get into a theatre to see a German propaganda film that was being shown to Portuguese officers and civilians, but because we were obviously English-speaking we were refused admittance. When we inquired of a Portuguese officer who spoke English as to the reason, he replied, after making inquiry at the wicket, "You are English." We replied that we were North Americans, and he said, Well, that is the same thing." We were not permitted to enter. I say therefore that when we have equipment of this kind we should be very careful where we send it.
_ The government was quite right in answering the third part of this question by saying that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the extent and nature of aircraft exports to the United States, and I shall not make any further inquiry as to that.
I turn now to something which concerns this country. In April I was in the United States. I had been invited to address certain meetings, principally a teachers' institute in Michigan. While I was there I was much disturbed to learn that the prestige of Canada was not as high as it should be. There was a tremendous amount of criticism of this country. Just before I went to the United States I had read in the newspapers of an attack upon Canada by two commentators in Washington who complained of our attitude in relation to the Alaska highway and in relation also to air routes, for what I thought to be United States military aeroplanes, into the northern part of Alberta. I made some inquiry of the Department of External Affairs before I left here, so that if the 
matter did come up while I was there I would be in possession of the facts. ' I was glad I had done that because I found that the statements to which I refer had been widely publicized and were based on an entire misrepresentation of the truth.
The minister will recall that on March 13 a story appeared in some of our local newspapers with regard to a transportation problem that had presented itself, and I asked the minister a question about it on the orders of the day. The question was, as recorded on page 1288 of Hansard of March 13:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Munitions and Supply. Has he an article in to-day's issue of the Toronto Globe and Mail blaming him for impeding the flow of war materials by United States trucks to eastern points across Canadian highways" If so, will he inform the house regarding the matters complained of in the article?
In his reply the minister gave the background of the story and the problem. I entirely supported the policy that was followed prior to the war, and will support that policy now if it is shown to be in the interests of Canada and the war effort of the united nations.
I hope the minister will not regard what I am going to say as personal criticism or even criticism of the policy. I say it merely because I want to get this situation cleared up. I believe and have always believed and have often said in this house that the railways of Canada are the lines of communication upon which this country has been built, that the railways are the bands of steel, as it were, which bind the provinces together and that we cannot afford to allow our railways to fall into disrepair or to be deprived of the sort of business that will enable them to handle the heavier and unprofitable freight that must be carried from one end of this country to the other. I have said, and I want to repeat, that I believe that the whole transportation system of this country should be under public control, and that when buses and trucks operate they should not be permitted to compete with and destroy the railway system upon which this country must depend for its major problems of transportation. They should be used to feed the main lines of traffic; they should be used to supplement rather than to compete with the railways of this country.
A violent attack was made in the House of Representatives of the United States a few days ago upon Canada and upon the Minister of Munitions and Supply in particular. I suppose their procedure is different from our own, because I imagine that if a member here were to begin to make an attack upon a public representative in the United States he would

War Appropriation-Supplies
be stopped. It would be considered to be a breach of the courtesies due to a friendly people. I am not going to read all this statement; I do not know whether the minister has seen it, but I shall give him the copy from which I read and ask him to explain the situation. If the explanation is satisfactory, then I think publicity should be given to the minister's reply. This statement was made by Representative John D. Dingell in the House of Representatives a few days ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: They do not necessarily have to make speeches; they can file them.

That is probably what happened in this ease. However, his remarks received quite wide publicity in the Detroit News and other newspapers. As I said before, I think there is much misunderstanding on the other side of the line of the situation in this country, and, if I may say so, something should be done about it. Every member of parliament and every public man in this country who receives an invitation to address a public body in the United States should fed it his duty to accept the invitation. I think that should be done by all of us who receive these invitations from time to time. The statement reads in part:
It must be evident and startling to the patriotic American people and their Canadian friends to the north, to learn that this one-man opposition-
Tha-t is the minister.
-is responsible for the loss of time in transporting essential war materials urgently needed at the front and that the time lost via' the longer roundabout way along the southern shore of Lake Erie between the points mentioned of Port Huron, Detroit, and Buffalo amounts to anywhere from six to ten hours per trip, and it is conservatively estimated that there is a waste of 35,000 transportation days per annum, plus millions of tire miles and an additional uncalculated loss in the consumption of gasoline. The savings in mileage, mind you, between Detroit and Buffalo over the Canadian route, as compared with the longer all American route, is the difference between 261 miles [DOT] and 365 miles or a saving over the Canadian route of 104 miles per one way trip. The difference between Port Huron and Buffalo, using an all American route, as compared with the short and direct Canadian route is the difference between 210 miles and 420 miles or a saving of exactly fifty, per cent or 210 miles per one way trip.
That is the story told to the American people. I continue:
Why should the American people sacrifice the use of their automobiles, tires and gasoline? Why should they forego the comfort of oil heat in their homes this coming winter only to have these essentials squandered needlessly because of an unpatriotic, autocratic, and brazen attitude on the part of a railroad spokesman clothed in the official robes of Minister of
Munitions and Supply? This selfish railroad opposition, centered in Mr. Howe as regards this question, is the very same opposition which stood in the way of the completion of the Alaskan highway so essential to the defence of the entire west coast of continental North America and which was only recently broken by the rising tide of adverse public sentiment. The delay incurred has caused incalculable loss and exposed our peoples to great danger.
At another point he said:
American tankers, and more important, American lives are being sacrificed every day to supply the deficiency caused by the useless consumption of millions of gallons of gas which could be saved by the use of the approved Canadian route.
Toward the end of his remarks he went on to say:
I think it is timely to suggest that this problem might become one for the congress to investigate. I am thinking, Mr. Speaker, that it may be well to consider the appointment of a select committee of the house with the power to summon such witnesses as Lieutenant-General William S. Knudsen, J. B. Eastman, Director of Defense Transportation, Milo Perkins, Chairman of the American Section of the Joint War Production Committee of the United States and Canada, and others, in order to obtain first hand information with regard to the stricture which exists. In concluding my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I want to make it clear that every responsible official-
I draw attention to this.
-of the governments of the United States and Canada who has examined the problem has agreed that this short Canadian route is essential and must be utilized.
The point I wish to make now is that on March 13, in reply to a question asked by me, the minister pointed out quite briefly the background of the situation. Ever since 1937 when our railways were in the doldrums and when we had cars of all kinds to spare he said that this organization of trucking interests has been endeavouring to get the right to transport across Canada goods which originate in the United States and are destined to points in the United States. The minister said, as reported on page 1288 of Hansard:
I may say, however, that the representations have always come from parties interested either in building the trucks or in selling the gasoline or operating a toll bridge or toll tunnel. I have never seen representations from potential users of the service.
Was any official reply to that statement made in the House of Representatives?

Not that I know of. This was sent to me and I know of no official reply to it. Accompanying it was information to the effect that this important subject is and has been for some considerable time under consideration by the joint war production
War Appropriation-Supplies

board of the two countries, and that on January 26 our own Canadian section of the board approved the suggestion.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Not true.

Not true?
Mr. HOWE. No.

And on March 16 the joint board approved the suggestion on the ground that the United States railways and highways cannot handle the war material originating in Michigan and destined for Buffalo and points beyond.
I express this opinion: If it is true that the United States railways cannot handle the traffic; if our Canadian railroads cannot handle the through traffic and there is a material saving in mileage and in every other way in transporting munitions by the Canadian route, we should give not only every consideration to but every facility for the movement of war goods by a Canadian route. I do not know what the railway situation is in this country. I have with me a statement showing that there is a shortage of railway cars, trucks and so on in the United States, for the movement of such goods. I understand that recently the United States railways asked congress for
218,000	additional cars for this year to enable them to move the material which must be nloved at this time. My information is that they were allowed 18,000, as a matter of fact, and that this year they have notified Mr. Eastman that they require 380,000.
I do not know what our railway situation is. I do not know whether the Canadian lines from Detroit east to Buffalo are able to cope with an additional amount of traffic of this description. But I do think that if the situation is as has been outlined in this representative's speech, that is to say that the American roads are congested, the railways overburdened, and the haul 50 per cent greater through the United States, some plan should be worked out to give them the right to move these goods through Canada via a Canadian route. But may I add that under no circumstances should any group be allowed to use the war as a lever to get into this country and to utilize the Canadian route for their own purposes when the war is over. If they have a case in this time of war, and if the statement as I have read it to the committee can be substantiated, I am sure we should do something to meet the traffic congestion and to assist them by the use of the Canadian route.
This I want to say again, that we should do nothing at this time which would in any degree alienate the sympathy or opinion of any of the people of the United States. I feel that there has been misunderstanding-and graver mis-

understanding than I was aware of until very recently. This kind of thing, allowed to go unanswered if it is wrong, and unmet if it is right, is doing a grievous injury to Canada, to the relations between our two countries and to our war effort generally. I hope the minister will be able to clear up the points which have been raised in the United States House of Representatives.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I find myself a little confused by the statement of my hon. friend. I thought he was strongly pressing for the opening of the route for United States trucks, up to the last two or three minutes of his speech, at which time he seemed to reverse his position.
No, no; I was not doing that at all. I thought I had made my position clear.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Does the hon. member suggest they should go through?
I am drawing attention to it only in the public interest. I am not in a position to judge as to the merits of the case, and I am not taking any sides.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I see.
I wish the minister to understand that clearly. I believe the matter should be cleared up in the public interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
All right. I have given a
brief outline of the position to which my hon. friend has referred. Of course the bringing of my name into the discussion, so far as the press from outside is concerned, is purely gratuitous. As Minister of Transport from 1935 to 1939 I presented to the government the views of the railroads. I was myself virtually a railroad man at that time. In 1939 I was transferred to the Department of Munitions and Supply, and the subject does not affect in any way that department. It is a matter really for the Department of National Revenue. An order in council or a change in customs regulations is necessary, and I assume the only possible opposition to it would be from the railways. But certainly, incidental to my position as Minister of Munitions and Supply, I have no views at all. Whether a change in the customs regulations was made or not would not affect by one iota the operations of the Department of Munitions and Supply. The view, of course, has been that of the government, and to single out one particular member of the government and call him a one-man bottleneck is more or less gratuitous.
The fact of the matter is that a group of Canadians are promoting this monopoly in transportation across this particular stretch

War Appropriation-Supplies
of territory. They were very active in Canada for two or three years, and then they discovered that much more effective propaganda in Canada could be carried out from the United States, with the result that for the past two years the headquarters of the organization has been in Washington.
The inventor or sponsor of this project was a man named Corelli, a Canadian born in Winnipeg, and associated with the automotive business, first in Montreal and I believe later in Toronto. He conceived the idea that a material saving in transportation costs could be worked out by diverting highway traffic between Buffalo and Detroit over the Canadian highways, and that the shorter distance would permit a profit being made by whoever had a franchise to operate the shorter distance. He organized a company called International Highway Forwarders Limited. I believe his principal associates were the British American Oil Company, General Motors, and one or two others. I mention the fact that they were interested in selling gasoline or motor trucks. I believe everyone concerned had some rather direct interest in the affairs of the company, in that way.
Representations were first made in 1936. In the session of 1937 a bill changing the customs regulations was introduced in the senate. It did not however emerge from the senate. I believe it was 1936-37, although it may have been 1937-38, that I appeared before committees of, each house and, as it was my duty to do as Minister of Transport, expressed the views of the railways. When the company moved to Washington some United States interests were added.
I think one man is either the president or the director of the Peace bridge, and there are other interests of a similar nature. Arrangements have been worked out, I think, under which International Forwarders Limited have a contract with a very large number of trucking concerns in the United States. The first plan was that the Canadian company would have its own trucks and drivers and convey the vehicles across Canada, but I think the present arrangement is that International Forwarders Limited will furnish the drivers for the American trucks and drive those trucks across Canada for a fee.
There are other features besides competition with the railways. There are five lines of railway between Buffalo and Detroit, operated for the most part with Canadian crews. In a time of depression it is something to think about, to set up a competing line of trucks with no investment in the route and a free franchise to divert as much traffic as possible to the highways. It is also something to think
about to set aside a certain section of our country to be a bridge between two large industrial centres. The passage of trucks across this strip of territory would bring no prosperity to that territory. The people there would simply be residents on a bridge between two large cities. The highways there were not built for traffic of the kind, and various opinions are expressed as to whether they are suitable for continuous heavy truck traffic. I believe a report has been produced on the other side of the line which indicates that the highways are suitable. The chairman of the transport commission is making an investigation now on behalf of the Canadian government of all aspects of the situation and I assume his report will express an opinion on this subject.
It is a situation that has some very attractive features. On the other hand I do not like- this is only a personal view, and I have never expressed it as a reason why I do not want to see this traffic-a little group of citizens setting up a monopoly on our highways. I do not think that is a desirable way to use the public domain. I also dislike very much condemning people who live along the highway system which would be used under this proposal to be faced with a steady stream of heavy trucks over the highway which their children must cross, and which they also must use for access to other places. These are the objectionable features. Whether they are sufficient in a time like this to be maintained, I cannot say. The government has asked the chairman of the board of transport commissioners to conduct an inquiry into all phases of the situation and report to the government what action ought to be taken. That report will be presented shortly, and the government will take such action as it may consider wise.
Have any official representations been made by the United States government that this traffic be allowed?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
No official representations. Unofficial representations have been made from rather high quarters, but nothing in an official way.
Bringing in the Alaska highway was, of course, purely gratuitous. The facts about that highway are these. We received an inquiry from the United States as to whether arrangements could be made to survey a route across Canada. We answered promptly, almost the same day the inquiry was received, and gave a favourable reply. We were ready with our tractor trains to take in gasoline to permit the survey to be made as soon as a decision was arrived at. As soon as the United States decided to make a survey we cooperated in

War Appropriation-Supplies
every way possible. There was never a doubt in anyone's mind that if the United States wanted a road across Canada, Canada would do all it could to make that road feasible, and that is being done. Canada has acquired the right of way for the road and is assisting the United States in every way to carry out its plans.
So far as the use of the airways to Alaska is concerned, it has been understood from the time Canada entered the war that the Alaska air route, which was built by Canada-the airports are the property of Canada and have been developed as part of a very important air route-should be free for the use of United States military planes. There is an international convention which provides that if a civilian plane wishes to use that route permission must first be obtained from the state department of the other country. A plane from the United States entered Canada without any permission being asked. It had radio equipment, and it was announced at Winnipeg that it was to do transport work for the United States government between Edmonton and Alaska. We thought we would like to know a little more about this, so we grounded the plane at Edmonton and made inquiry of the United States government and asked what this was all about.
