I happened to be going to Washington at the time and I made personal inquiries there. I found that everybody there had assumed that someone had asked Canada for permission for this plane to fly, and it was explained that the army wished to engage this air line to do certain transport work. The necessary permission was given that very day. I telephoned back to Ottawa and was able to convey full permission to the army to use this civilian transport company. The whole delay amounted to only about four days, and was caused by the fact that no one in the United States had advised Canada what She wished to do in that connection. My hon. friend knows how these stories get abroad. Canada was in the war when the United States was at peace, and the isolationist element in the United States thought it good business to advance their cause by very unfair criticism of Canada and its war effort. But I think that everyone in an official position in the United States fully appreciates what Canada is doing in the war. I may say that we have been able to be very helpful to the army and navy and air force of the United States from the fact that we had been in the war longer than they had, and had our production of munitions and war equipment further advanced than theirs. I think that that help has been appreciated as the finest sort of cooperation in war production between Canada and the United

States. We confer with the United States authorities frequently and have a number of joint committees which are working on common problems. But there is a weakness in our publicity arising from the activities of the isolationist press before the United States entered the war.
I agree with my hon. friend that no opportunity should be lost by Canadians visiting in the United States to correct any wrong impression that might prevail over there, either by speaking in public or otherwise. I myself spoke before the Boston chamber of commerce three or four weeks ago in an address which was broadcast over the New England network, and I received an astonishing number of letters from people who were surprised by what I was able to tell them about Canada's war effort. Hon. members will do a real service to Canada if they accept every opportunity to do likewise.
I hope I have covered the ground my hon. friend wished me to cover. The matter to which he refers is being examined in the light of the war situation. Of course he will understand that any army truck or any war truck can pass freely. It is purely a matter of shipping merchandise in bond over that route.
It would be war material, would it not? That is what I had reference to.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I suppose it would be any material; it is any material that would be required to pay duty in Canada. Of course there are certain classes of war material that could pass in any event, because the goods would not be dutiable, into Canada. Any goods can move that way if those concerned are willing to pay duty at one end and get a refund at the other end. It is simply that they wish to pass the goods through in bond. But I understand the permission that is being asked for is for any goods to move from one point to the other, whether war materials or not; and I do not know whether we can distinguish between what are war materials and what are not, because most materials may be used either for one purpose or the other.

Merchandise consigned to wholesale or retail companies doing business in other than war materials would not be war materials. Goods consigned to factories or organizations doing war work might be considered as such. All I can say is that I hope consideration is being given to this matter, and that if it has merit, the request will be granted; if it has not, I hope it will be refused.

War Appropriation-Supplies

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think I can add anything to this, but I am going to give something of my own experience in this matter.
As the committee knows, I was Minister of National Revenue between 1935 and 1940, and it was upon the Minister of National Revenue that the lobby converged for the concession desired. There is a section of the Customs Act which provides that goods can move in bond in Canada only on railways. That is an old section, and it has been argued that it is obsolete and should be amended. On the other hand, the customs officials of the Department of National Revenue have always felt that there were solid reasons for the maintenance of that section in its present form. The reasons are these: that if goods move in bond on a railway the cars are sealed; the minimum crew of a train is five, I think; the train is always on the tracks and you always know where your goods are; whereas, if goods were permitted to travel around in Canada, and through Canada, by truck coming in at one point and going out at another, the danger of goods on which duty had not been paid going into circulation in the country would be very greatly increased. That was the argument which was always advanced by the officials of the customs division, when I was Minister of National Revenue, against any change. Added to that was the undoubted wish of the railways, and I may say that the representations were not all on one side. In the year when this lobby was at its height we received numbers of resolutions from railway workers locals along the line of the railways; and I know the Canadian National Railways were very much disturbed at the prospect of an alteration of the rule that foreign goods on which the duty has not been paid, which have not entered in customs, should not move other than on the railways-and this for obvious reasons.
In two years the representatives of the interests who wanted to get this concession came to Ottawa and did everything they possibly could to have that section of the Customs Act amended. I remember that on one occasion they brought along a large red truck, parked it outside the parliament buildings here, and invited myself as Minister of National Revenue, and perhaps other ministers, to inspect the truck and satisfy themselves that it was safe to move goods across the country in that type of conveyance. There was one year when a bill was introduced in the senate; it went before one of the senate committees, and conflicting representations were made. But the view of the
government always was that the relevant section of the Customs Act should not be amended.
As my colleague has said, there is no reason in the world why he should be singled out for attack in this manner. The natural target is the Minister of National Revenue, although I am not suggesting that he should be attacked. I believe I took full responsibility during the years when the matter was before the government for deciding not to recommend an amendment of the act. Whether there has been a change in conditions recently which would justify a change in the law I do not know, but the committee should not be under the slightest illusion as to the reasons behind the agitation. The only reason I have for speaking now is to add my testimony to what my colleague has said. The reasons behind this agitation are those of men who want to make money out of getting the use of these highways for the running of their trucks.

May I interject this?
I am not asking that anything should be done that would give these people entry into Canada. If we can assist in the movement of war goods across Canada, well and good. Anything which is done will be done, I hope, only as a war measure and for the duration of the war, and then only if we cannot handle it in any other way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are two other matters to which I want to refer briefly. The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) this afternoon, on the orders of the day, corrected a statement which he made last night in reference to the number of subscriptions for victory loans. His speech of last evening, while not precisely accurate in regard to the figures* was substantially so; but the correction he made this afternoon is substantially incorrect. I have had a word with him, and I think he is satisfied that that is so; it was an inadvertence on his part. I should like to put on record the true figures. I am assuming that the population of Canada is 11,420,084: that is the preliminary census total as released by the dominion bureau of statistics. On that basis the ratio of subscribers to population for the first victory loan was 8-48 per cent, and for the second victory loan, 14-72 per cent. The number of subscriptions in the first victory loan was 968,259, and in the second victory loan, 1,681,525.
The other matter I wanted to mention is one which was being discussed early this afternoon, and that is an alleged agreement between an official of the Department of Munitions and Supply, the director-general of aircraft production, and treasury officials or the
War Appropriation-Supplies

treasury, to the effect that certain expenditures by companies would be allowed as part of their costs of production or part of the overhead. I made very careful inquiry, and I am assured by the comptroller of the treasury that no agreement of that kind was made. He has made inquiry also of his officials; and therefore all that I can say is that there must be some mistake about there having been any arrangement with the treasury that these particular expenses would be allowed as part of the overhead. It may be that they would have been on general principles, and it may be that some discussion of general principles took place or some assurance in regard to the general rule was given; but that is a matter as to which an opinion could not be formed until the actual expenditures, whatever they were, came in. They would be subject to review, subject to audit by the officers of the treasury, but I do not want it to go out to the public that this particular class of expenditure was the subject of any agreement between the treasury and anybody.

First of all I wish to congratulate the hon, member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) upon his constructive address this afternoon dealing with the oil resources of Canada and the possibility of developing oil sands. He has gone to a great deal of trouble and taken a good deal of time, and altogether he shows commendable interest in personally examining these oil resources. I am glad that the minister has taken steps to see if these can be developed as a war necessity, as a great Canadian resource for the future. I am also pleased that the minister and his officials and engineers are investigating the oil shales of New Brunswick. I hope they will also be developed. I pointed out yesterday that there were also extensive oil shales in Nova Scotia, which to some extent have been explored. They are to be found in different parts of that province, in the county of Pictou, in Antigonish and other places. I believe there are great possibilities.
While discussing the matter of oil and gasoline, I think the minister should make a statement-I do not believe it has been made officially yet by the oil controller-as to the position of tourists entering Canada, more particularly in the maritime provinces. Some publicity has been given to the statement that they will be allowed only twenty gallons of gasoline on coming to Canada. If that is correct, it will mean that they can cover only three or four hundred miles, and that would completely destroy the motor tourist traffic in Nova Scotia, Prince Edward

Island and other parts of Canada in the coming year. If that is necessary owing to the exigencies of the war we shall have to abide by it, and the traffic will have to be diverted by rail; but it would be well for the minister to make a definite statement. There are many people depending on the tourist traffic, and they have to make provision for the coming season.
I wish to refer now to the discussion with respect to Mr. Ralph Bell, director-general of aircraft construction. May I pay him my respects and express my appreciation of the wonderful energy he has shown and the great accomplishments he has achieved in connection with the aircraft industry of Canada. Canada, the empire and democracy the world over are under great obligations to certain men. Among these are Lord Beaver-brook and, in a not much lesser degree, such men as Mr. Ralph Bell. There may have been some indiscretions; his methods may have been a little more direct than others, but his purpose cannot be questioned. When one realizes the responsibilities that have rested upon him since he has been in this position, one must be amazed at what he has accomplished.
The minister said that the aeroplane industry had increased four hundredfold.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I should have said forty, and I had the correction made.

I would almost accept four hundredfold as correct, because in some particulars it is correct. Even if it is only fortyfold, it is an immense expansion, and that falls largely under the responsibility of Mr. Bell. One cannot realize the difficulties under which he and those associated with him have laboured in this connection, building these plants from the very beginning, having them established, with one or two exceptions, as new plants, getting the personnel together, accumulating the materials, and so on, This has been a great undertaking. After the designs have been fixed upon, jigs constructed, materials obtained, delays and disappointments overcome, the planes are constructed so that they will be worthy of the Minister of National Defence for Air Services and our splendid airmen, who are in the forefront of the fighting wherever our battles are to be won.
The immensity of the work carried on by the aircraft industry can be realized only when one considers the total figures. I go to the Financial Post for these figures. I am sorry that many of them are not available to hon.

War Appropriation-Supplies
members. We are under obligations to the Financial Post for much information that is adduced in the house. In the edition of April 25, just a few weeks ago, it was reported that the aircraft industry had already totalled $391,719,381, and that the new orders that have been placed since the beginning of the year, the first three months of 1942, total the enormous sum of $86,500,000. Mr. Bell's purpose was to build up the morale of the aircraft industry, and we are all in agreement with him in that purpose.
In the town of Amherst we have accomplished a great deal. We were the last, I believe, to undertake the construction of the Avro-Anson, and we were the first to have machines, built in that plant, flying. I have been waited on from time to time by representatives of the workmen there, and one of the last statements they made to me was that without additional help they would be prepared to increase the output of that plant very materially if they could get the materials in sufficient quantities and if a few changes were made. They are as anxious as the minister and the director-general of aircraft production to get production, and while a pep-up of morale may help the industry in Amherst, I do not believe it is necessary. I believe they are anxious to do all they possibly can.
We are all agreed that one of the greatest responsibilities rests on those who have to supply materials and direct the aircraft industry, and we are deeply obligated to Mr. Bell and his associates for what they have done, for the present programme, and for what we expect they will do before the termination of the war.
The minister in making his statement gave figures of capital assistance to war industries. He stated that it had reached 380 million dollars. About a year ago I understood him to say that capital assistance to war industries amounted then to 268 million dollars. In November in his statement to the house it was 550 million dollars. So I do not reconcile the figure of 380 million dollars. I do not think he gave the portion of the two billion dollar appropriation that is earmarked for the Department of Munitions and Supply. It was stated that 997 million dollars was earmarked for the army, 259 million dollars for the navy and 585 million dollars for the air force, plus 40 million dollars contributed by the other members of the commonwealth air training plan, a possible additional 300 million dollars which the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power), said would probably be required, and 21 million dollars for sundries.
I see the minister's figure is in this report of March 17, 335 million dollars for the Department of Munitions and Supply.
These are enormous figures, but hon. members willingly vote these estimates if they are being used for the main purpose, that is winning the war. The minister also reported that he had expended, from the beginning of the war up to the present time, four billion dollars. These are enormous sums and the people of Canada have accomplished a great deal. I am not in entire agreement with the hon. member for Invemess-Richmond (Mr. McGarry)- although I usually agree with him-when he said that sufficient consideration has been given to the outlying parts of Canada and to Nova Scotia in the distribution of war industries. Much more could have been accomplished, and I believe that in fairness much larger expenditures should have been made in Nova Scotia and other outlying parts of Canada. At this time the minister and the government could very well adjust the inequalities in industrial enterprise in Canada by locating industries in the maritime provinces, that have suffered grievously in regard to industrial activity. Twenty-five years ago there were many small industries in Nova Scotia that were more or less prosperous. They have carried on under great disadvantages in recent years, due to the growth of mass production in central Canada and the tendency of the big industries to absorb our smaller industries and to dump their products in the outlying parts of Canada, making unfair competition for our local industries. There are many industries necessary in a time such as this to produce special war supplies, industries that would have some surviving or permanent value after the war, industries that must be sponsored or encouraged by the government; such industries should be located in places like Nova Scotia.
With regard to the matter of shipbuilding, while much has been done in the last six months or so I still feel that sufficient consideration has not been given to the old shipbuilding province of Nova Scotia. I agree with the statement of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), that ships and more ships are needed to-day. Last session I repeated the call made by Lord Beaverbrook to the four comers of the earth that ships and more ships are required, appealing to the people everywhere to supply ships. I said at the time that more consideration should be given to Nova Scotia in respect of shipbuilding, wooden shipbuilding, using Nova Scotian raw materials rather than teak, mahogany and imported woods, and using diesel-engine power. While we do not want to waste money
War Appropriation-Supplies

or make unnecessary expenditure, I believe it is in the interest of the situation we have to face that more activity be shown in this connection.
Senator Duff protested against the refusal of the department to undertake a wooden shipbuilding programme in Nova Scotia. He said, as reported in the Halifax Chronicle of March 26, 1941:
With proper men in charge of the effort, there was no reason why fifty Nova Scotia shipyards "from river John around to the Parrsboro shore" should not be started on wartime shipbuilding within a month's time. . . .
The senator advocated the building in Nova Scotia of not only wooden corvettes, minesweepers and patrol boats, but also "small cargo boats propelled by sail and diesel engines capable of carrying between 1,500 and 2,500 tons of cargo." Despite the preference for steel ships, the urgency of the situation would undoubtedly make a place for wooden cargo ships in the war effort, he said.
Wooden ships have three great advantages in the present crisis, Senator Duff argued.
I quote Senator Duff because he has spent his life in connection with shipping and the sea.
I want to commend the minister, although he was perhaps a little later than some of us would have liked, for what has been done in resurrecting the steel plate mill in Sydney. That mill, I understand, is now producing plates for shipbuilding. I hope that further shipbuilding yards will be established in Nova Scotia. I understand there is one in construction now,, perhaps two, and if more interest had been shown earlier in the war I believe steel shipbuilding in Nova Scotia could have been increased manyfold.
We have no record of what has been done in the different parts of Canada as regards shipbuilding, and I was disappointed that the minister refused to give any reply to a question that I asked in the house on this subject. On March 25 I made these inquiries with respect to shipbuilding, as reported on page 1615 of Hansard:
1.	What is the number, the total tonnage and the estimated cost of all ships ordered built by the government of Canada or by any other government to be built in Canada of 100 tons capacity or more for commercial purposes, since September 10, 1939, in each of the following provinces, (1) Nova Scotia, (2) New Brunswick, (3) Prince Edward Island, (4) Quebec, (5) Ontario, (6) British Columbia?
2.	What is the number and the total tonnage of all ships launched in each province to March 14, 1942?
The minister's reply was:
This question asks for total production in a certain line of war effort. I have no objection personally to giving the information, but we have been asked specifically by the British government, and an agreement has been entered into on the part of the British government, the 
United States government and the government of Canada, not to give total production figures of war materials.
This is information to which hon. members are entitled. I do not see, in view of the announcements made concerning the shipbuilding programme, why hon. members are not entitled to at least some information in respect of this very important matter.
In the Financial Post that I quoted a few minutes ago it was stated that the shipbuilding being undertaken in the first three months of this year represents an expenditure of $86,500,000. I have here a semi-government publication, at least one that is sponsored by the government, that is issued under their patronage. The April issue of the Canadian Geographic Journal states that 154 cargo boats, 153 life-saving craft, 1,059 life boats, 614 light craft, 300 steel naval craft and 925 patrol boats have been built. These figures include 154 cargo boats of 10,000 tons deadweight, and 18 cargo boats of 5,000 tons. The total cost was $275,000,000.
They indicate where these ships are being built. It would seem that information is given out indirectly through these government or semi-government publications and through newspapers and periodicals which we are denied in the house. I feel we should have this information, at least to a greater extent than we have up to the present. There are many places in Nova Scotia and the maritime provinces where shipbuilding activities could be undertaken and I believe splendid results would be obtained.
I am most sympathetic with the minister in solving the problems that arise in connection with the Department of Munitions and Supply. The people of this country and the members of this house have given him unbounded support. I think the members of the house have been of assistance to him by pressing for further activities with respect to shipbuilding, with respect to tanks, with respect to aeroplane engines, with respect to aeroplanes and many other war manufactures. It is the task of the members of this house and the members of the official opposition to be helpful to the Minister of Munitions and Supply and to all the defence ministers in carrying out their responsibilities in this war. If there has been any criticism it is that they have not proceeded fast enough, that they have not done enough, that they have not been as frank with us as they should have been in giving us information as to the requirements of the army and the other services. The members of the opposition are anxious to contribute to the uttermost in assisting the government in the

War Appropriation-Supplies
responsibilities that are theirs in carrying on the war. I am appreciative of what the Minister of Munitions and Supply has done. I sympathize with him in the responsibilities that have arisen and I often wonder how one small head can hold all that the minister knows.

Mr. Chairman, on a question of privilege, the Minister of Finance has made a statement, and before he made it I discussed with him the remarks I had made. In looking over my notes and in looking over the press report I am now in the position of asking that a correction be made of a correction. I now find that the figures I gave last night were as reported in the press, and I therefore ask that they remain as given. However, I thank the minister for the official information he has given.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I think I should reply to the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) particularly in regard to the gasoline situation in the maritime provinces. I have no personal knowledge of the Nova Scotia shales, but I shall be glad to refer his remarks in that connection to the oil controller with the request that he send me such information as is available. With regard to tourists, the present situation is that the tourist will be given a book containing four coupons when he crosses the border. My hon. friend says that he is to be given twenty gallons of gasoline, but that does not follow automatically; he will be given four standard coupons.
To-day that would be twenty gallons?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: Yes, but to-morrow not so good. I am sorry to say that the situation in the maritime provinces has deteriorated to such an extent that the oil controller finds it necessary at midnight to-night to cut the value of coupons in the maritime provinces to two gallons. We hope that this will be temporary and that the value of the coupons can be increased. But there just is not enough gasoline to go around.

Does that
apply only to the maritimes?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
Yes, that is all. In order
to work out the situation without hardship, in order to distribute fairly what gas is available to the motorist, it is necessary for the time being to honour coupons only to the extent of two gallons. The authorities in the United States quite reasonably take the view that if they are curtailing their travelling for pleasure in the United States, it is not desirable for United States citizens travelling in
Canada for pleasure to have any better treatment than they would receive at home. Similarly, I think our own citizens would resent the use of gasoline for pleasure purposes by tourists when gasoline for pleasure driving in Canada is being severely restricted. What can be done for the tourist beyond the four coupons that he is given at the border will depend on circumstances. If he has come to Canada simply for pleasure driving I doubt if anything further can be done for him, but if he is travelling to a summer home in Canada, it is probable that provision may be made to take him to his home and bring him back by his giving the proper information to the nearest representative of the oil controller. I do not wish to be too definite about that, but I believe that is the present situation.
I am glad my hon. friend has mentioned the director general of aircraft production, and I think that every word he said about Mr. Bell is well justified. It is unfortunate that a man with the temperament of Mr. Bell finds it difficult to abide by the conventions of government business. He occasionally makes an indiscreet slip of the type which has been discussed by the committee, but those slips are made wholly from his desire to get on with the job. He is a little impatient with our red tape, and I think hon. members should view the situation in its true light, which is just that.
With regard to shipbuilding in the maritimes I may say that we are anxious to build more steel ships there than we are building. We find it impossible to get sufficient staff to man the two largest shipyards, the Halifax shipyard and the Saint John shipyard, in order to enable ship construction to proceed while ship repair work is being done. We have made every effort to bring these staffs up to the point where both shipbuilding and ship repair work can proceed. Experience has taught us that up to this time this has not been possible. Naturally when repair work is required it must take precedence. The quickest way to get merchant tonnage is to repair the ships you have, rather than to divert men to the building of new ships. I cannot believe there is any supply of shipbuilders in the maritimes that has not been tapped. If there are such men able to work on ships, men who might be called ship mechanics, I urge them to report to Halifax, Saint John or Pictou, where they will be welcomed. They are badly needed in the existing yards and will be put to work immediately. I can see no purpose whatsoever in opening additional shipyards, when we cannot man the yards we have.
War Appropriation-Supplies
If the men so report, will provision be made to cover their expenses from wherever they happen to be to the point of operations?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I think any shipyard in the maritimes would be glad to pay their fares there. The Saint John Dry Dock Company advertised in every western paper that they would do that for anyone in the west. I believe inquiries should be made, however, as to whether they are still willing to do it, and I would suggest that if my hon. friend knows of anyone who wishes to travel there he should ask that person to communicate with the Saint John Dry Dock company.
It would relieve the men of all that anxiety if they would also pay their fares back, in the event of their being rejected.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I do not know that that is exactly fair. The men offering themselves should be fairly sure they are able to do the work, before they put the company to the expense of transportation to the maritime provinces.
Otherwise the men would have to bear the brunt.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: We do not like people to come down as tourists. If they can do the work, then they should work. We do not want to encourage the tourist industry in that way, simply by saying that if they do not like the looks of things they may go back, and have their fares paid.

There is one thing I do not understand in connection with the shipbuilding programme. We are very grateful to British Columbia for what has been done there, but I do not understand why there should be seventeen of these yards established in British Columbia, when in Nova Scotia this work is so belated. It places eastern Canada at a great disadvantage, and I do not understand it.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
Offhand I would say there are more yards in Nova Scotia than in British Columbia. I believe there are more than seventeen yards building some kind of ships in Nova Scotia at the present time, and I understand those yards have been busy continuously since the shipbuilding programme was begun. Many ships have been built in the maritime provinces-although I have not the figures before me. I dislike breaking down 
the figures by provinces, because, after all, this is Canada's war effort, and it does not matter much to Canada's war effort whether they are built in one place or another.
We are grateful to British Columbia for what they have done, but I think more might have been done in Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: But I say if there is any man in Nova Scotia able to work on a ship, he could do the war effort a great deal of good by reporting to one of the three big shipyards, where we have been continuously short of men.
Would they have to be skilled men?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: If they are able-bodied they can be trained; that is my opinion.

I understand that in these days ministers: responsible for the prosecution of the war are looking around for facilities, and for raw and manufactured materials to contribute to the war effort. Is the minister aware of the fact that at Glencoe, in my constituency, there is a large deposit of magnetic ore proved, by analysis, to be of very high quality? A man has been paying the rentals on the leases for several years. Last year the Dominion Coal company became interested in the area, did some work and, in fact, produced some ore. I was talking to the engineer of that company, and he told me that a large amount of the ore could be recovered by surface mining.
A few days ago I received a letter from the man holding the leases stating that the Dominion Coal company have given up their interest in the property, and that he is now prepared to produce a thousand tons weekly. I have no doubt he has made the same submission to the hon. member for Cape Breton South who, I am sure, will have something to say on the matter. The man in question is seeking some assistance from the Department of Munitions and Supply and, as he points out, that assistance would not need to be very great. If assistance is not given it would appear that this man, who has been carrying the leases for a number of years, will likely have to surrender the property to the Dominion Coal company.
I would ask the minister to take the matter under consideration, and see if something could be done, or some assistance could not be given this man who has continued to hold on to this valuable property.

Questions
He is not asking for very much to-day, but wishes only the initial facilities necessary to bring about a production which, I have no doubt, can be greatly increased in the future. Has this matter been brought to the minister's attention?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext:
I have no personal knowledge of the iron deposits mentioned by the hon. member, but I shall be glad to obtain a report from my steel controller, and consider what can be done to bring that iron ore into the war effort.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Crerar the house adjourned at six p.m.
Monday, May 18, 1942
